steps.body: To compare two DIFFERENT fractions, you don't always need a common denominator. Use **1/2 as a stepping stone**: if one fraction is less than 1/2 and the other is more than 1/2, the bigger one is obvious — no matching bottoms required.

widget.prompt: For each pair, match which fraction is BIGGER using 1/2 as the stepping stone.

pairErrors.feedback: That answer belongs to 3/8 vs. 5/9. For 2/7 vs. 5/8, doubling shows 2/7 falls short of 1/2 while 5/8 clears it — 5/8 is bigger.

widget.missFeedback: Double each numerator and compare to its own denominator — one falls short of 1/2, the other clears it.
widget.successFeedback: In every pair, one fraction sits below 1/2 and the other above it — the stepping stone settles it instantly.

explanationVariants: 7/15 doubled is 14, short of 15 — less than 1/2. 9/16 doubled is 18, past 16 — more than 1/2. So 9/16 is bigger.
One falls below 1/2, the other rises above it — no common denominator needed.

steps.body: Sometimes both fractions land on the SAME side of 1/2 — both above, or both below. The stepping stone alone can't separate them then; you'll need a finer method (like cross-multiplication) to finish the job. Spotting WHEN the shortcut works is half the skill.

explanationVariants: 3/5 doubled is 6 (more than 5) and 4/5 doubled is 8 (more than 5) — both land above 1/2, so the halfway trick alone can't separate them.
Same side of 1/2 means you need another method here.

hints: Check both fractions against 1/2 using the doubling trick before deciding.
If one fraction is below 1/2 and the other above, the one above wins — sort it left or right.
If both fractions land on the SAME side of 1/2, the halfway trick alone can't say which is bigger — that's the 'can't tell' group.
explanationVariants: 9/16 (above 1/2) beats 7/15 (below); 4/7 (above) beats 5/11 (below); 7/10 (above) beats 5/12 (below). But 3/5 and 4/5, and 5/9 and 6/11, are each two fractions above 1/2 — same side, so 1/2 alone can't settle those two.
Opposite sides of 1/2 settle a pair instantly; same side means you'd need a finer method, like cross-multiplication, to decide.

steps.body: A stepping stone, not a detour.
takeaways: If one fraction is below 1/2 and the other above, the comparison is settled instantly.
If both land on the same side of 1/2, the halfway trick alone isn't enough — use a finer method.
Recognizing which case you're in is the real skill.

concept.body: Quick rewind. Check each fraction against 1/2 using the doubling trick. If one is below and one is above, the bigger one is obvious. For 2/5 vs. 3/4: 2 doubled is 4 (less than 5, so below 1/2); 3 doubled is 6 (more than 4, so above 1/2). 3/4 wins.
